distinguishing_features: Physical wheel geometry change: asymmetric tread profile modifying the contact-stress field, versus software-only monitoring inferences in all prior art
Progressive depth relief channels (10 mm x 20 mm, 15° offset) machined into the tread to accommodate deformation
Remedial mechanical redesign that redistributes Hertzian contact pressure rather than detecting a downstream symptom via existing telemetry
Pass/fail deformation test on a physically modified component, not a signal-indexing threshold
parsed.objective_technical_problem: How to reduce localized cyclic plastic deformation (wheel squat) and abrasion-erosion at the wheel-rail contact under high-load heavy-haul operation, treating the spatial contact-stress distribution itself as the lever rather than monitoring earlier indicators.
parsed.viable_reason: The physics check is internally inconsistent and physically implausible: removing material via relief channels and an asymmetric profile reduces the contact patch, which would raise rather than lower peak Hertzian pressure, and the claim that reducing semi-axis a by 30% lowers P_max to 840 MPa ignores the coupled reduction in b and contact area (P_max ∝ 1/sqrt(ab)), plus a deformation threshold referenced to a fabricated '1% of channel depth' has no basis.
parsed.non_obvious_reason: No prior art discloses a geometric tread redesign producing a stress-path redistribution for squat resistance, so this departure is not a routine parameter change to any of the monitoring-based references.
